prompt: In the MESI protocol, what does the Invalid (I) state mean for a cache line in a given core's cache?
choices: The data is stale but can still be used for reads
The core holds the only valid copy of the line in the system
The line does not contain valid data and must be fetched before use
The line is currently being written back to memory

prompt: Core 0 holds a cache line in the Modified (M) state. Core 1 issues a BusRd for that same line. What must happen before Core 1 can get a correct, up-to-date value?
choices: Core 0 must flush/supply its dirty data (writeback or cache-to-cache transfer), then both lines settle in Shared
Core 0 simply invalidates its own copy without supplying any data
Core 1 fetches directly from DRAM and ignores Core 0's cache entirely
Nothing — a BusRd targeting a Modified line is ignored by the snooping core

prompt: In the worked trace (C0 reads counter, C1 reads counter, C0 writes counter, C1 reads counter again), both caches hold the line in Shared right before C0's write. What is C0's state immediately after that write, and what bus transaction does it issue?
choices: State becomes Modified; C0 issues BusUpgr since it already holds valid data and only needs to invalidate the other copy
State becomes Exclusive; C0 issues BusRd to refetch the data
State stays Shared; no bus transaction is needed for a write
State becomes Modified; C0 issues BusRdX to refetch data it already has

prompt: Two threads each increment a separate uint64_t field in a shared struct, 8 bytes apart, with no padding, so both fields fall in the same 64-byte cache line. What is the primary cause of the measured slowdown?
choices: The increment instruction itself runs slower when executed on multiple cores
The shared cache line continually ping-pongs between Modified in each core's cache, forcing invalidation and reload traffic on every write even though the two threads never touch each other's data
The compiler fails to vectorize integer increments on struct fields
TLB misses dominate because the struct crosses a page boundary

prompt: Which change actually eliminates false sharing between two hot fields written by different threads?
choices: Marking both fields volatile
Padding or aligning each field so it lands on its own 64-byte cache line
Wrapping both fields in atomic<uint64_t> without changing their layout
Reordering the struct's fields alphabetically

prompt: In the store-buffering (SB) litmus test — Core 0 runs x=1 then reads y into r1; Core 1 runs y=1 then reads x into r2; x and y both start at 0 — real x86 hardware can observe r1==0 and r2==0. Why is this possible despite x86 being described as strongly ordered?
choices: x86 allows StoreLoad reordering: each core's own store sits in a local store buffer and may not be globally visible yet when that same core executes its load
x86 does not implement any cache coherence protocol
This result only occurs due to compiler reordering at -O0, never on real hardware
x86 reorders StoreStore operations, so the two stores could execute out of order

prompt: What does pairing atomic_store_explicit(&flag, 1, memory_order_release) with atomic_load_explicit(&flag, memory_order_acquire) guarantee that plain, unannotated store/load would not guarantee on a relaxed-ordering machine?
choices: That the store executes faster than an ordinary store instruction
A happens-before relationship: every write issued before the release-store becomes visible to any thread whose acquire-load observes that stored value
That the store bypasses cache entirely and writes straight to DRAM
That the cache line holding flag can never be evicted while the lock is held

prompt: Sequential consistency, as defined by Lamport, requires that:
choices: There exists a single global total order over all cores' memory operations, consistent with each core's own program order, where every load sees the most recent store to that address in that order
Each core may reorder its own operations freely as long as the final results happen to be correct
Stores are always instantly visible to every core, but loads are allowed to return stale values
Only atomic operations must be globally ordered; plain loads and stores are exempt from any ordering requirement
